extracted.intended_audience: news journalists and editors reporting on transgender and gender-expansive people and issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journalists on language, sourcing, visual choices, legal/medical context, and ethical practices when reporting about transgender and gender-expansive people across beats (health, crime, sports, immigration, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify sources by the name they wish
rubrics_metrics.description: Always identify sources as they wish, even if obtaining records on a person requires asking for their deadname.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legal and preferred names differ — e.g., incarcerated people — use the name the source uses. See deadnames guidance for handling birth names respectfully. If records require the deadname for verification, obtain and report the preferred name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant anonymity to at-risk incarcerated sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider granting anonymity to trans sources in prisons and jails, especially those not openly trans, because they may be at substantial risk for violence or retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity is particularly important for incarcerated people who could face retaliation. Evaluate safety risk before identifying sources; use anonymity when disclosure increases danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain explicit consent for ongoing communication with incarcerated people
rubrics_metrics.description: Take extra care to obtain consent for ongoing communication and publication from incarcerated people, as most of their communications will be monitored by prison staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that contact with journalists can place incarcerated people at risk. Clarify what communications are permissible and whether publication could endanger the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider interplay between gender identity and carceral policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how gender identity interacts with carceral rules and policies; the same policy may affect trans women, trans men, and nonbinary people differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating or ignoring experiences of nonbinary and trans men. Report on how sex-segregated housing rules and other regulations are applied to different identities; provide subgroup-specific implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generalizing experiences across trans subgroups
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on issues involving trans communities at large, be careful to avoid generalizing the experiences of one subgroup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make distinctions between subgroups (trans women, trans men, nonbinary) where relevant; do not assume experiences are uniform across all trans people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear, medically accurate language for transgender health care
rubrics_metrics.description: Health care that trans people seek out as part of their gender transition is a type of medical care; use clear phrases like 'gender-affirming care' or 'transgender medical care' as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer phrases like 'gender-affirming care' are acceptable; shorthands such as 'trans health care' are acceptable in headlines. Strive to use medically accurate names of surgeries and treatments where necessary, and use the language a person uses in direct quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid asking unnecessary or grossly invasive medical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: If describing a specific person’s medical care, avoid asking grossly invasive questions or including unnecessary detail for shock value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about genitals, hormones, or procedures only if essential to story’s purpose. Consider whether similar details about cisgender people would be considered relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume all trans people experience gender dysphoria or seek medical care
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all transgender people experience gender dysphoria or have a diagnosis; they seek varying and individualized forms of gender-related medical care, and many never receive care due to cost, access, or choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generalizations about treatment or dysphoria. Report the diversity of experiences and barriers to care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize how classification affects access to care
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurance billing processes, hospital policies, or state laws may classify the same medical care as 'gender-related' for one patient but not another, affecting access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how administrative classifications — not only biological differences — determine who can receive care. Note that anti-trans laws often rely on these classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gender-neutral, medically-accurate phrasing in health coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Medically accurate language referring to humans and their anatomy is sufficiently gender-neutral; use simple gender-neutral words over neologisms when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer words like 'patients' or 'people' when appropriate. Avoid forcing neologisms when an existing neutral term (e.g., 'firefighter' over 'fireperson') is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate gender and anatomy; use anatomy-based phrasing when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid equating gender and anatomy; consider who is affected based on relevant anatomy (e.g., people with ovaries, people with prostates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise phrasing such as 'people who can get pregnant' when anatomy is central. Use gendered words like 'women' only when study/population warrants it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with euphemisms like 'people who menstruate'
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'people who menstruate' may be inaccurate if used as euphemisms for all cisgender women and trans men, since some groups (postmenopausal women, trans people on testosterone) do not menstruate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure such phrasing fits the population being described; prefer specific medical terms where clarity is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use less-common body-language terms only when sourced directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'chestfeeding' or 'birthing people' are not universally endorsed; use them only in direct quotes from people who use them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implying broad endorsement of nonstandard terms. If translating or explaining terms across cultures, consult the source first.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use gendered medical language
rubrics_metrics.description: If discussing a study that only includes cisgender women, it is most accurate to use gender-specific language (e.g. 'pregnant women'); if transgender men or nonbinary people may be included, consider phrasing like 'women and other patients'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match language to study inclusion criteria and be explicit about who was included in research findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether protected health information is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing about transgender people, consider whether it’s necessary or appropriate to ask about their genitals, hormones, or medical procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask only if it sheds light on the importance of care or barriers to access. Refer to 'asking irrelevant questions' guidance. Avoid collecting PHI for sensational reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain nuance around detransition and retransition
rubrics_metrics.description: Detransition has several meanings and is not synonymous with transition regret; reporting should reflect varied personal meanings and study definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify how individuals and studies define detransition/retransition. Do not assume detransition equals regret; report reasons people stop transitioning (lack of support, resources, identity changes, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and report methodology/definitions in studies on detransition
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical studies and literature reviews may use different metrics to define detransition; when writing about studies, understand and relay their definitions and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read study definitions and methods; if unclear, contact authors to avoid misrepresenting findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise terminology for hormone therapy
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender-affirming hormone therapy (also called cross-sex hormone therapy) is a form of transgender medical care; avoid references to 'male hormones' or 'female hormones' and refer to the specific hormone where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terms like 'masculinizing' or 'feminizing hormone therapy' where appropriate. Note puberty blockers are not considered cross-sex hormones in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report individual variability in hormone therapy
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no singular model for hormone therapy; people undergo hormone therapy for varied personal or medical goals and on differing schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray hormone therapy as individualized; avoid implying a single 'right' regimen or timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'reproductive health' over 'women’s health' when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'reproductive health' for topics like abortion, birth control, and menstruation because these issues can affect trans men and other transmasculine people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use medical terms (abortion, pregnancy, testicular cancer) to provide specificity when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize the expertise of quoted experts in sports reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain and contextualize the specific expertise of sources quoted as experts when reporting on trans athletes; not all doctors are experts in trans health or sports medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether a source’s expertise is academic, philosophical, political, or medical; prefer authors of scientific literature and athletic/regulatory bodies for technical questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize interviewing trans athletes themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize talking to trans athletes, the population most directly impacted by sports-related legislation and policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center voices of those affected; use their perspectives alongside expert analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply proportionality in sports stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Note how many trans athletes have actually attempted to compete in contexts affected by regulations; many laws target populations with very few trans athletes competing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implying widespread participation if only very few trans athletes are involved. Explain potential impacts on funding/procedures that affect all players.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about claims of competitive advantage in youth sports
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little data directly comparing trans athletes’ performance to cisgender peers, especially in youth/non-elite sports; emphasis on competitive advantage may be inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the limited evidence base and avoid overstating physiological advantages in non-elite contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report on testosterone-related regulations with scientific caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on rules that use testosterone thresholds, note that there is no straightforward measure of 'normal' testosterone for any gender and limited research on performance impacts for trans athletes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain specific policy thresholds, their scope (may include intersex athletes), and the scientific limitations in linking testosterone levels to performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid umbrella-label imprecision with 'transgender athletes'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'transgender athletes' can be shorthand but may inaccurately imply only trans women are affected; laws may affect trans men, nonbinary people, or those categorized by birth-certificate sex markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about which groups a law or policy affects and how nonbinary athletes may be categorized differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'drag' only for performance art contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'drag' or 'being in drag' to describe merely dressing in seemingly gender-incongruent clothes, and do not call someone 'in drag' or a 'drag queen/king' if they are not a drag performer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize many drag performers are cisgender; ask performers for preferred names/pronouns. Use stage/drag names when appropriate and defer to the performer’s wishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer to drag performer’s identity and stage name preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify and defer to a drag performer's wishes regarding names and pronouns; if unreachable, opt to use drag/stage name over other names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that ballroom performers have complex gender concepts; avoid assuming a direct mapping to cis/trans categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous focus on a trans person’s appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid descriptors (height, voice pitch) that call attention to assigned sex at birth or fetishize/exoticize a person; avoid 'before-and-after' pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use appearance details if they are pertinent and not invasive. Avoid labeling features as masculine/feminine/androgynous unless source uses that language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accurate historical and cultural context
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish trend pieces that imply being trans is a new phenomenon or a youth fad; evidence exists across time, age groups, and cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sensationalizing changes in data-gathering as population changes; include historical context where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never knowingly deadname in obituaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Never knowingly deadname a trans person in posthumous news coverage, including obituaries; reprinting birth name alongside current name is profoundly disrespectful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write around a deadname when handling posthumous legacies; use phrasing that respects the person’s chosen name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask asylum seekers about gender language and identification preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on transgender asylum seekers, ask about pronouns, titles, and how they describe themselves; be aware of language/cultural differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a source uses a term in another language, consult them before translating. Double-check last names before publication to avoid jeopardizing asylum applications; do not assume asylum motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stigmatizing language when reporting on sex work
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'sex worker' over 'prostitute' or 'escort' and provide context about disparities without stigmatizing people who do sex work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify names/pronouns and which details are on/off the record; be mindful some use work identifiers different from legal names. Explain socioeconomic drivers and avoid demeaning language even in quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'same-sex marriage' when legal status matters
rubrics_metrics.description: In the U.S., use 'same-sex marriage' to reference marriages where both partners have the same legal sex marker, rather than 'gay marriage' or 'same-gender marriage', when legal status is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain complexities when trans people's legal sex markers differ from gender identities, and be precise about which documents/state standards are being used to determine legal sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'losing a loved one' cliche for coming-out stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid framing friends' or family's processing of a coming out as 'losing a loved one' unless the trans person has died.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center the trans person's experience; do not make family grief the story’s focal point when inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat polling data carefully and check methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Polling can lend context but quality varies; avoid drawing conclusions beyond the specific question asked and review sample size, weighting, and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize question wording effects (e.g., 'Is changing one’s gender morally wrong?' vs. 'Do you favor laws banning certain care'). Interview pollsters when possible and avoid overgeneralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider safety risks when publishing images from criminalizing regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources in regions criminalizing trans people may be at increased risk from images or videos; consider how an image could endanger a trans person or loved ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with depicting children and consider in-camera techniques (silhouetting) to obscure identity. Even public testimony may carry different risks when published widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain informed consent for photography in private or sensitive spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: In spaces with a reasonable expectation of privacy (e.g., medical clinics), photojournalists should ask for and receive clear, informed consent before taking or publishing identifying photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If consent cannot be obtained or is denied, do not use the image unless there is an extremely compelling reason. The same applies to embedded social media images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never republish sensitive medical photos without explicit consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Never republish or embed sensitive medical photos of a trans person’s body without that person’s explicit consent, and weigh news value even if consent is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware surgical photos are sometimes reused as shock imagery; avoid republishing them without clear, informed consent and strong news justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include only verifiable identity information in cutlines
rubrics_metrics.description: In cutlines, only include information that can be verified about someone’s identity; do not assume a person’s presence at a trans event means they are trans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If identity is ambiguous, use neutral descriptors like 'A protester at a rally for trans rights' or 'a person in a green wig'. Maintain context for file photos reused later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid identifying individuals as trans in crowd shots unless confirmed
rubrics_metrics.description: In crowd shots, avoid identifying specific people or groups as trans unless the group is explicitly made up only of trans people; do not broaden to 'LGBTQ+' unnecessarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate drag performers or gender-nonconforming people with trans people without confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove or censor deadnames/misgendering in video where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: For video, avoid using portions of clips that include deadnaming or misgendering; alternatively, notify viewers that the person is being misgendered and drop the sound rather than 'bleep' it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit archival footage sensitively to avoid perpetuating deadnaming and misgendering; removing the audio is preferred to bleeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use file photos and B-roll with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using file photos that make a specific trans person or portrait stand in for transness broadly; use conceptual imagery when appropriate and retain accurate cutlines if images are reused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reusing hyper-specific portraits as generic art. For conceptual pieces, consider pride flags, statehouses, illustrations, or collages instead of a person's portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate stock images
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid stock photos that falsely imply medical abuse or are easily misconstrued; stock images of unidentified people who 'look' stereotypically queer are usually poor choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stock images that depict models who are actually trans or nonbinary when showing trans people, and avoid images that could mislead about treatments or experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify context and on/off-the-record status for sex work sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on trans people engaged in sex work, confirm what details are on the record and off the record and clarify identifiers the source wants used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many sex workers use work identifiers different from legal names; be explicit about consent for names/details, and do not publish information that could jeopardize safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify legal definitions and document reliance when reporting on marriage law
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on marriage law involving trans people, be precise about which legal sex markers and documents are being used and how courts/agencies may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how differing document standards (driver’s license vs birth certificate) and the adoption of 'X' markers can complicate legal status reporting.
